  "text": "In September, Mara found a jar of tomato sauce on her doorstep. Her brother had tied a strip of red thread around the lid. On the label he had written, in careful block letters, FROM YOUR GARDEN.

She called to thank him. He said he had made too much and asked whether the plants were still producing. A few, she told him, though the nights were getting cold. He offered to come by on Saturday and help pull them up when they were done.

He arrived with their father’s scissors in his coat pocket. They spent the morning gathering the last green tomatoes and cutting the stems away from the fence. Her brother worked slowly, stopping once to sharpen the blades on a stone. Mara set the tomatoes in a cardboard box and carried it inside.

At lunch, they warmed the sauce and ate it with bread. Her brother said their father used to save seeds on folded pieces of newspaper. Mara remembered the papers drying on the windowsill, each one marked with a date but rarely a name.

After he left, she looked through the box. Some tomatoes had begun to blush. She placed those on the kitchen sill and wrapped the rest in newspaper, one by one. The garden outside was bare except for the two short sticks, still standing where she had first pushed them into the ground.

She left them there. In spring, she thought, she might use them again."
